1.pericope_label: A false balance is abomination to the Lord: when pride cometh, then cometh shame: riches profit not in the day of wrath

schools.summary: Henry makes honest dealing a test of religion, since he is not an honest man who is not devout nor a godly man who is not honest, catches the excuse that a blot is no blot till it is hit, holds that a man of fixed principles need not tack about every time the wind turns, and insists that riches will neither put by the stroke of death nor ease the pain, much less take out the sting.

Gill holds that there may be common honesty without the grace of God but no grace of God without honesty, answers the proverb on pride with a list of instances running from the angels that sinned to the fall of Rome Papal, orders three guides for the upright in the Spirit, the word and the sincerity of the heart, and reads the day of wrath as the judgment that overtook Rome Pagan and will overtake Rome Papal.

Clarke explains the false balance mechanically, as a beam with one end longer than the other so that it turns sooner at one end, and reads the proverb on pride psychologically, the proud man being repeatedly mortified because he is never treated according to the worth he assumes while the humble man can only be disappointed by praise he never desired; Wesley glosses the balance as all false weights and measures in commerce.

Keil and Delitzsch treat the terms, making abomination a participial noun that transfers abhorring to the thing done, rejecting three modern derivations of the word for perverseness in favour of the Jewish lexical tradition, defining the day of wrath as the day when wrath breaks through the limits of long-suffering, and insisting that the smoothed way is evenness of surface rather than straightness of line; Ellicott argues from the repetition of the proverb that false weights had grown common as the commerce of the nation developed.

debates: What does the word opposed to integrity mean? Keil and Delitzsch canvass three modern derivations, two from Arabic verbs meaning to step out and to turn about, which they call improbable, and a third from a verb meaning to smear, which would yield slipperiness and which they judge scarcely admissible; against all three they set three Jewish lexicographers who gloss it as wavering, falsifying and misrepresentation. Ellicott, without argument, takes the same word in the sense of covering a matter up.
outliers: Ellicott dates the proverb from its own repetition, arguing that a warning repeated three times in the book points to a form of cheating that had grown common as the commerce of the nation developed.
Clarke describes the rigged balance as a piece of hardware, a beam with one arm longer than the other, where the others treat it only as a figure for dishonest dealing.
Henry states the sinner’s own defence before answering it, that men think there is no sin in that by which money is to be got, and that while it passes undiscovered a blot is no blot till it is hit.
Gill ends a list of proud men brought to shame with a contemporary application, the fall of Rome Papal, where the others keep to the ancient instances.
themes: a beam with one arm longer than the other
honesty as the foundation under religion
pride mortified by its own expectations
a word fought over by lexicographers
riches that cannot take out the sting

6.pericope_label: The righteousness of the upright shall deliver them: when a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish: when it goeth well with the righteous, the city rejoiceth

schools.summary: Henry pictures the hypocrite wrapping himself in his hope as the spider in her web and distinguishes the worldling who must leave the world he expected to continue in from the hypocrite who comes short of the world he expected to remove to; he answers the eighth verse with three deliverances in which the persecutors came in the place of the men they had condemned, and observes that even those with no great stock of religion have a good word for a good man.

Gill counts what perishes with the wicked man, the expectation of longer life, riches, honour and pleasure, and the expectations others had of him; applies the hypocrite of the ninth verse to false teachers and their heresies; and dates the rejoicing of the city to the days of Constantine when persecution ceased and to the reformation when the pure doctrines of the Gospel were revived.

Clarke notes that hope was not made for the wicked and yet they most abound in it, holds that the word rendered hypocrite would be better translated infidel since it describes not a pretender to religion but a man who disbelieves revelation and lives in pollution, and makes the good man a blessing to his neighbourhood by his example, his advice and his prayers; Wesley reduces the deliverance to escape from the infection of the hypocrite’s evil counsel.

Keil and Delitzsch describe the godless man as one who rocks himself in measureless hopes, record an ancient version that reverses the seventh verse so that it is the righteous whose hope survives death, enter the objection that experiences of the opposite kind to the eighth verse are not wanting since divine justice shows itself here only as a prelude, argue that the word rendered hypocrite means in ancient Hebrew the man resolved upon evil, and take the city of the tenth verse for the state; Ellicott allows two senses of the eighth verse and takes the blessing of the upright to be chiefly their prayers for the people they live among.

debates: Does the seventh verse say what the versions say it says? Keil and Delitzsch record an ancient version which turns the clause round, making it the righteous man whose hope does not perish when he dies, and observe that this is the converse of the received text; at the ninth verse they report three old translators who rendered the disputed word hypocrite, its later sense, and refuse to emend the text against two scholars who would, since the reading as it stands lay before every other translator. Clarke, without reference to the versions, reaches a similar conclusion about the word by translating it infidel.
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch are the only voice here to admit that the eighth verse does not always hold, allowing that experiences of the opposite kind are not wanting because divine justice shows itself in this world only as a prelude.
Henry answers a general proverb with three particular deliverances, the gallows, the den and the prison, in each of which the persecutor came into the place prepared for his victim.
Clarke observes the irony that hope, which was not made for the wicked, is the thing they most abound in, hoping to be saved with their faces set toward perdition.
Gill supplies dates for the city rejoicing, the reign of Constantine and the reformation, where the others keep the proverb general.
themes: a hope no wider than the grave
the persecutor in his victim’s place
hypocrite, infidel, or the man resolved on evil
a proverb its own commentators qualify
prayers that exalt a city

12.pericope_label: He that is void of wisdom despiseth his neighbour: where no counsel is, the people fall: the merciful man doeth good to his own soul

schools.summary: Henry makes silence an act of friendship and holds that a man undervalues himself in undervaluing one made of the same mould, adds the one qualification to the duty of concealment, that the honour of God and the real good of society may require disclosure, argues from stewardship that a man must be just to his family before becoming surety for another, and sets the gracious woman beside the valiant man as equally honourable.

Gill supplies three motives for despising a neighbour, that a man thinks himself wiser, richer or holier, or else that the word means he wants a heart; explains the talebearer as a walking merchant who takes up wares in one place and vends them in another, noting two versions that render the word accuser; makes the leaderless people a ship without pilot or helm; and quotes Henry by name on Christ becoming surety for strangers and smarting for it.

Clarke contrasts the fool who brings his neighbour’s defects into the most prominent view with the prudent man who hides what he can and puts the most charitable construction on the rest, calls the talebearer a hawker and trader in scandal who will tell his own secrets rather than have nothing to say, and quotes the expanded version of the sixteenth verse to warn how careful a man should be whom he marries; Wesley reduces the second clause of the twelfth verse to bearing reproaches patiently.

Keil and Delitzsch hold that no German or English expression quite covers the contempt described in the twelfth verse, answer a scholar who mocked the maxim about many counsellors with the proverb that too many cooks spoil the broth, report an ancient translator who read a different word at the sixteenth verse and added a line about a woman who hates the right being a throne of dishonour, and reject the interpreters who reverse subject and predicate at the seventeenth verse; Ellicott corrects the fifteenth verse to for another rather than for a stranger.

debates: Is the seventeenth verse about the effect of kindness or the evidence of it? Keil and Delitzsch report many interpreters who reverse subject and predicate, so that the man who does good to himself is presumed kind to others because charity begins at home, and reject the reading: in by far the greatest number of cases the man who denies himself nothing is an egoist in relation to others, while the man who denies himself lawful enjoyments is capable of self-denial for others. Clarke keeps the plain sense and observes that no man can show a disinterested mercy without improving his own moral feeling.
outliers: Gill quotes Henry by name, the only voice in this chapter to cite another of the commentators, taking his observation that Christ became surety for strangers and smarted for it but was not broken by the payment.
Keil and Delitzsch answer a critic who dismissed the maxim about many counsellors with two popular sayings, that too many cooks spoil the broth and that he who asks long errs.
Henry qualifies the duty of keeping a secret, allowing that the honour of God and the real good of society may require a matter to be disclosed.
Clarke reports a saying of common speech about the cruel man, that he frets his flesh off his bones, and observes that such men are seldom seen in good health.
themes: contempt with no name in two languages
a peddler who deals in secrets
a maxim mocked and defended
a commentator quoting a commentator
mercy that returns upon the merciful

18.pericope_label: The wicked worketh a deceitful work: though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: as a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion

schools.summary: Henry makes the deceitful work self-deception, the sinner building on sand and cutting his own throat while the sin smiles on him; holds that numbers and unanimity in sin will not protect the sinners, since it will not excuse a man to say that he did as his company did; allows that beauty is itself a jewel of gold where there is grace to guard it before lamenting the waste; and takes the expectation of the wicked as the desire for a woeful day in which they may fish in troubled waters.

Gill reports a Jewish commentator who reads the joined hands as hand to hand, the reward of their work passing from the hand of God into theirs; takes the emblem of the twenty-second verse from the practice of ringing swine with iron to stop them rooting, so that a gold ring is unbecoming and soon carried to the mire; and keeps the last proverb to its first clause, that good is what the righteous man continually desires and what he has here and hereafter.

Clarke says nothing the wicked man does is durable except his crimes, argues that godliness promotes health and lengthens life while the wicked live not out half their days, cites a traveller on the Hindoos ratifying an engagement by laying one right hand on another, and quotes an old English version of the twenty-second verse in its original spelling; Wesley answers the same verse with eight lines of verse addressed to the woman herself.

Keil and Delitzsch canvass the versions at every turn, a Latin translator making the second half of the eighteenth verse independent, two eastern versions making fidelity itself the reward, a Greek version reading a righteous son at the nineteenth, and another spoiling the emblem of the twenty-second by supplying as and so; they identify that verse as the first emblematic proverb of the book and read the last word of the twenty-third as presumption rather than wrath, which Ellicott also does, while Ellicott further offers three senses of the joined hands and dates the nose-ring to the earliest times.

debates: What does the expectation of the wicked come to? The received reading makes it the wrath of God, and Henry keeps it, describing men who desire the woeful day so that judgments may remove those who stand in their way. Keil and Delitzsch doubt that the word can be taken so here and prefer its other sense, want of moderation, so that the hope of the godless is presumption; Ellicott takes the same view and adds that they do not ask in the way or for the things God wills.
outliers: Clarke leaves the text for ethnography, citing a traveller on the Hindoos ratifying an engagement by laying one right hand upon another, the only voice here to look for the gesture outside the Bible.
Wesley, who elsewhere in this chapter writes in half-lines, answers the jewel in the snout with eight lines of verse addressed to the woman herself.
Keil and Delitzsch identify the twenty-second verse as the first emblematic proverb in the book, where the two lines stand to each other as figure and import.
Gill reads the emblem from the swine rather than the jewel, noting that swine are ringed with iron to stop them rooting, so that a gold ring on such a creature is soon carried to the mire.
themes: a sin that smiles while it kills
hands joined four different ways
an emblem every voice adds to
a nose-ring still worn in the East
wrath or presumption

24.pericope_label: There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth: he that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: he that trusteth in his riches shall fall

schools.summary: Henry supplies the figure of corn increased by being sown, works out how a man grows poor by meanly sparing until his industry is cramped and his credit destroyed, turns the twenty-sixth verse into a rule that men with stocks of corn should sell at the market price and not aim to make a gain of the judgments of God, and makes trusted riches a broken reed that runs into the hand of the man who leans on it.

Gill notes that four versions add the words his own to the scattering, insists that the blessing soul bestows good things and does not merely wish them, reads the withheld corn as the withheld Gospel and names the forbidding of preaching and the locking up of the Scriptures in an unknown language, and has the man who trusts his riches falling as leaves fall in autumn.

Clarke holds that the man who distributes in the right spirit gets more good than the poor man who receives the bounty, and marvels that God gives the property, gives the heart to use it aright, and then recompenses the deed; he adds to the curse of the people the curse of God, a canker in the money in this life and in the soul throughout eternity; Wesley glosses the section in half-lines, giving liberally, being enriched with temporal and spiritual blessings, and selling upon reasonable terms.

Keil and Delitzsch prefer the traditional reading of the twenty-fourth verse against three codices, derive the word for blessing from the idea of spreading out so that blessing is causing increase by word and deed, identify the hoarder as the corn-usurer a prophet describes, distinguish three synonyms for seeking by their roots, and see behind the last verse a withered tree and a tree whose leaf is always green; Ellicott answers the twenty-fourth verse with an old epitaph and grants at the twenty-sixth that the dealer’s selfishness may in the long run benefit the community.

debates: Is the corn dealer simply to be cursed? All of them say so, and Keil and Delitzsch identify him with the usurer a prophet denounces, while Henry lays down the rule that a man with stores should be content with moderate profit and Clarke adds the curse of God to the curse of the people. Ellicott alone pauses to grant the argument on the other side, that the truth of the proverb is not affected by the fact that the dealer’s selfishness benefits the community in the long run by limiting consumption as the price rises.
outliers: Ellicott answers a proverb about giving with an old epitaph, that what we spent we had, what we saved we lost, and what we gave we have.
Clarke states the return on charity as a strict inequality, that the giver gets more good than the poor man who receives the bounty.
Henry itemises the ways of growing poor by saving, unpaid debts, a family left without what is convenient, and goods lost for want of the expense that would have preserved them.
Gill turns the hoarded corn into hoarded doctrine and names the withholding of preaching and of the Scriptures in a known tongue as the famine meant.
themes: giving that increases the giver
an epitaph in three clauses
the corn-usurer and his defender
rising early to do good
a withered tree and a green one

29.pericope_label: He that troubleth his own house shall inherit the wind: the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life: behold, the righteous shall be recompensed in the earth

schools.summary: Henry reduces the troublers of a house to two extremes, an anxious earnestness that is niggardly at home and keeps up feuds within the family, and a want of common prudence that ends in servitude; holds that what such men get is not only empty as the wind but noisy and troublesome; makes the righteous trees of life and the wise trees of a commanded knowledge; and notes that this is the only proverb here with a Behold prefixed, before admitting that many sins go unpunished on earth, which argues a judgment to come.

Gill lists every way a man may trouble his house, bitterness to a wife, provoking children, menacing servants, idleness, a worldly spirit that hurries business, a mean temper that withholds food and clothing, or profuseness; makes the fruit of the righteous what grows on Christ and is received from him; and prefers to read the recompense of the last verse as the chastisement of the righteous, which they have only in this world.

Clarke makes the man who dissipates his property as unsatisfied as one who feeds upon air, keeps the Hebrew plural of the tree of lives which increases the bodily and mental vigour of those who eat, and reports the Greek reading of the last verse that an apostle quotes word for word; Wesley makes the same man as unable to keep what he gets as to hold the wind in his hand, and settles the last verse in two words.

Keil and Delitzsch canvass an eastern version that renders the clause twice and a Greek version that makes the offender merely unsociable before deciding for a niggard, reject the Greek of the thirtieth verse for reversing the relation of fruit and tree, hold that the fruit is the righteous man’s activity itself and a tree of life for others, and explain the last verse as an argument from the less to the greater turning on a verb that may mean either reward or punishment; Ellicott takes the trouble of the house to be avarice and reports the same Greek reading of the last verse, naming three righteous men who were punished.

debates: What is the recompense of the last verse? Henry allows both a reading in which the righteous are chastised and the wicked fare worse, and one in which the righteous are rewarded and the wicked punished; Keil and Delitzsch note that the verb itself may mean either, denoting full requital of whatever kind; Gill gives both and prefers the chastisement, since the righteous have it only here. Clarke and Ellicott set the Hebrew aside for the Greek, which turns the verse into a question about where the ungodly shall appear if the righteous be scarcely saved, and observe that an apostle quotes that version rather than the Hebrew.
outliers: Gill answers a one-line proverb with a seven-fold list of the ways a man may trouble his household, from menacing his servants to sheer profuseness.
Henry admits against his own argument that many sins go unpunished in the earth and many services unrewarded, and takes that as evidence of a judgment to come.
Keil and Delitzsch reject a Greek rendering of the thirtieth verse on the ground that it grows the tree out of the fruit, which discredits itself.
Henry distinguishes the trees of the thirtieth verse, making the righteous trees of life and the wise trees of knowledge, and is careful to add that this knowledge is commanded and not forbidden.
themes: a household troubled seven ways
wind that is noisy as well as empty
fruit that is itself the tree
a verb that means reward or punishment
a version an apostle preferred
